The previous points describe a very demanding specification for extending the Max Architecture into a fully autonomous execution system, not a simple chatbot or planner. Its main goal is to create a persistent, stateful, selfcorrecting platform that can plan, execute, verify, repair, rank, and synthesize complex tasks end to end with productionready quality.[1]

 Core goal

The central objective is to evolve the system so it can perform complex work with high autonomy through proactive planning, persistent execution, intelligent tooling, and automatic selfcorrection. The requested end state is a complete productionready implementation, not a draft, demo, pseudocode sample, or partial architecture sketch.[1]

 System design

The architecture is defined as hierarchical and persistent, with a fixed operating stack that runs from goal parsing and ingestion through planning, orchestration, sandboxed execution, retrieval, verification, repair, ranking, and final synthesis. Every task must first identify the real goal, extract constraints and ambiguities, build a roadmap, decompose into subtasks, allocate tools and models, persist execution state, verify outputs, repair defects, rank branches, and then produce one final synthesized result.[1]

 Sandbox backbone

A nonnegotiable rule is that every task must run inside its own isolated Linuxbased microVM or Cloud Computer, treated as the mandatory execution substrate for the whole system. These sandboxes must support rootcapable Linux execution, shell access, browserbased computer use, arbitrary package installation, longrunning sessions, persistent storage, snapshots, optional exposed ports, and finegrained Zero Trust egress controls.[1]

 Models and orchestration

The specification assigns distinct roles to multiple models: GLM 4.7 acts as the fast ingress router, GLM 5.1 is the supreme final synthesizer, Claude Opus 4.8 is the toplevel orchestrator for autonomous build mode, and other models such as MiniMax, Mimo, Kimi, Gemini, and DeepSeek handle reading, extraction, parallel reasoning, recursive subagent spawning, multimodal interpretation, and councilstyle response generation depending on the task type. The system must switch between simple conversation mode and autonomous execution mode, with the latter supporting deep orchestration, largescale software generation, iterative repair, and distributed worker behavior.[1]

 Required capabilities

The platform must include persistent orchestration, taskstate storage, checkpointing, retries, recovery, verification pipelines, ranking pipelines, memory systems, retrieval pipelines, streaming token handling, bounded concurrency, branch evaluation, and final synthesis. It must support at least 300 recursively created subagents, each with structured metadata such as IDs, parent links, progress, confidence, verification scores, retry counts, checkpoints, toolsets, and assigned models.[1]

 Product scope

The requested output covers the entire product stack: backend, frontend, persistence, authentication, authorization, validation, security hardening, observability, caching, network resilience, concurrency controls, deployment, recovery, scalability, CI/CD, testing, and exact startup procedures. The backend must remain in one single productiongrade Python file containing APIs, services, orchestration, persistence, SSE or WebSocket streaming, sandbox integration, retry and recovery logic, ranking, synthesis, validation, and operational controls, while the frontend must provide live execution graphs, agent trees, logs, task views, verifier streams, ranking state, artifact handling, and longrunning execution UX.[1]

 Output contract

The prior points also define a strict delivery format: architecture summary, folder tree, dependencies, environment variables, production configuration, install commands, run commands, schema, migrations, backend file, frontend files, reverse proxy and process manager configs, containerization, CI/CD files, tests, deployment guide, startup sequence, and verification checklist. The definition of done is equally strict: the system is only complete when orchestration is persistent, execution is longrunning, sandboxing is integrated, verification and repair loops are active, at least 300 subagents are supported, SSE streaming is visible, state is persisted, ranking and synthesis work, frontend and backend are integrated, deployment is real, and the result is directly runnable end to end.[1]
